title: The Wrong Wanting
blurb: The man she thought she killed is alive and waiting, her slack is due before noon, and a hearing is about to decide what she really wanted.

blocks.text: The dead man is dripping on the Bureau's front-desk carpet.
He gives Stan his name as Lionel Pargeter. He discharged himself, he tells me, against advice. "Hospitals keep asking questions," he says, "and I have only the one."
He looks at the fid on my belt the way you look at an old dog that once bit you.
"What did you untie off me, Miss Brandt? I should like it back."
I have rehearsed a hundred conversations at this desk. I have nothing for this one.
I want to laugh, or cry, or shake his hand until it comes off, because he is alive and all afternoon I believed I had killed him. Instead I do the thing I know how to do.
"Mr Pargeter, I'm so glad you're—"
"Vertical," he says. "Yes. So is the hospital. It was most surprised."

"If you have a question about a repair," I tell him, "the Bureau has a complaint form for it. I'll file it myself, first thing tomorrow." I take a form from the rack by Stan's elbow and hold it out with my own pen.
He fills it in standing up, against Stan's desk, in a beautiful slanting hand. It is one line long.
"Did you know?" I ask him. "About the knot. That there was something inside it, under the umbrellas?"
"Not the faintest," he says, and hums a little tune while he caps my pen, the way I imagine a man hums when he is tuning a piano.
Stan says "Security" into his telephone, quite gently, and a guard in a wet cape comes in from the porch.
Mr Pargeter puts his hat back on. "I'll wait," he tells me. "I'm told I'm very good at it."
The guard walks him out into the rain, and I stand on the wet carpet holding his one line. It says: What did she untie off me, and may I have it back?
I don't sleep much. At five I give up and lie in the dark and think about the rule, because the rule is the one thing I'm sure of.

Slack falls on the keeper within a day of the dwell. It comes as one coincidence, the same weight as the knot, and it always falls against the grain of what the keeper means to do. My two strands have not fallen. So they will fall this morning, before noon, across something I want.
So I decide what I want. Carefully, on purpose, I choose small harmless things.

I want to walk to the tram stop and stay dry. I want the ten past eight tram. I say them out loud to the ceiling. If the slack has to go against something, let it go against an umbrella or a timetable.
I am going in early anyway, but not for the tram. I am going in for the drawer.

The bottom drawer of the old cabinet behind my desk has "Unfiled" on its label in my own handwriting. In it are two hundred and twelve complaints. They are copies of four years of complaints Registry stamped No Action and put away. I copied them because they come from the same few doors and stairwells over and over, and nobody would listen when I said so. Standards will be in Registry today, because of me, and Standards opens drawers. So I have a cardboard box folded flat under my arm, and that drawer is going to be empty before nine.
I walk to the stop under my umbrella. It stays the right way out. I stay dry.
The ten past eight comes at ten past eight, and Wilf is driving it.
"Bureau!" he says, delighted. "You look like you've seen a ghost."
"I have," I tell him. "And he filled in a form."

Wilf laughs as if I've made a joke, and I sit right behind his cab and tell him the man from the steps is alive, because I have to tell somebody and Wilf is the only person I know who will just be pleased. He is pleased.
I get off at Tallow Row at twenty-five past eight, dry and early, and I think: it's working.

Registry at half past eight is empty and smells of radiators. I unfold my box. I kneel. I have my hand on the drawer handle when the ceiling over the filing run makes a sound like somebody clearing their throat. A tile bulges. Then it comes down, and the water comes with it.
It's a pipe. Cold brown water, all at once, straight down onto the cabinets and onto me.

In five minutes there are men in yellow jackets everywhere. Their foreman is a big man with a mop over his shoulder, and he takes one look and starts hauling the bottom drawers out of the cabinets to save the paper.
He gets to mine first, because mine is nearest the water.

He yanks, and it comes right out of its runners and tips, and two hundred and twelve copied complaints slide out across the wet floor like a dealt hand of cards. Every one is stamped No Action. Every one has an address at the top, and the same addresses come round again and again for anybody who cares to look.
The foreman looks at them. Then he looks at me, on my knees, with my box.
"Keen to get in early, weren't you?" he says. "Brought your own box and all."
And I see it.

I spent the morning wanting a dry walk and a tram, and the slack didn't care about either, because I never really wanted them. I only said I did. What I wanted, the thing I got up at five for, was this drawer out of this room before anyone saw it. The rule is right. I knew the rule. I put it on the wrong wanting.
"I'm wrong," I say, out loud, to the foreman and the water. "I wasn't wanting the tram. I was wanting the drawer."
"Right you are, love," says the foreman, who has no idea what I mean, and goes to fetch a bucket.
It's only two strands. The book calls two strands trivial. It does not feel trivial, kneeling in it.

I am still picking copies off the floor when my supervisor comes in at ten to nine and stops in the doorway with her umbrella dripping. She looks at the ceiling, then the floor. She picks up the nearest sheet and reads the address at the top, and then the next one.
"Ila," she says. "Are these ours?"
"They're copies," I say. "It's the same few streets, if you lay them out. I can show you—"
"Don't," she says, not unkindly. She puts them in my box herself, every one, and takes the box away with her.
At nine the bell rings.

You hear it everywhere in the building, through the walls and up through the floor: the nine o'clock bell, nine strokes from the Tallow Row tower, steady as a pulse. I stand in an inch of water and listen to all nine. It has rung nine strokes at nine every morning for nine hundred and eleven years, and in all the Bureau's record it has never once varied. Never late. Never a stroke short or a stroke over. Everything in my life has changed since yesterday at noon, and the bell hasn't, and I am so grateful for that.
At two o'clock I go before Standards.

The hearing room has no windows. Three of them sit behind a long table: a chair with very clean cuffs, an officer with a file, and an officer with a bob. I ask the officer with the bob her name, because I'd like to know it, and she says that won't be necessary.
My docket lies on the table between us, dried and wrinkled, the ink run a little, my signature still clear.
"Clerk Brandt," says the chair. "A member of the public collapsed during your repair. Standards will establish whether your docket was valid. Tell Standards what makes a docket valid."
I know this better than I know my own address.

"The keeper signs it in their own hand," I say, "before the untie starts. They have to be sober, they have to understand what they're agreeing to, and nobody can make them. I signed it myself at the top of the steps before the fid went in. I'd had a cup of tea. Nobody made me."
The chair writes something down. "And if the docket were void?"
"Then the untier is the keeper," I say. "And the untier was me as well. So it would have fallen on me either way. But it wasn't void."
"Standards did not ask whether it was void," says the chair. "Standards asked what would follow if it were. Officer."
The officer with the bob comes round the table and asks me to hold out my hands, palms down. She swings the bob above them on its silk. It goes round once. It goes round again. Then it settles.
"Two," she says.
"Two certified," says the officer with the file. "Two fell. Matching."
"It fell this morning," I say. "A pipe burst over Registry. I can tell you exactly how—"
"Standards does not require the shape," says the chair. "Standards requires the number."
"There's something in my remarks, though," I say. "The bob gave a half-turn before it counted. There was something inside that knot. I think it was holding his—"

"Standards has read your remarks," says the chair. "Remarks are not findings. The hospital's note records an old injury to the man's chest and a heart that ought to have failed years ago. Standards finds the collapse natural." He turns a page. "The complainant asks what was untied off him and whether he may have it back. Standards does not return things. Standards finds the complaint a crank. The Lantry Steps matter is closed."
I did it properly. The docket held, the count held, and the book held me up like a floor. I could hug the chair.
"Thank you," I say. "Thank you so much, really—"
"One further matter," says the chair.
The officer with the file turns to a new page, and I know my supervisor's handwriting upside down.
"Two hundred and twelve copies of closed complaints," he reads, "removed without authority and kept in an unofficial drawer. Standards considers this a misuse of records."
"They cluster," I say. "By address. The same doors, year after year. If somebody would only lay them out—"
"Standards is not asking what they say," says the chair. "Standards is asking why they were in a drawer."
I don't have an answer that isn't the truth, and the truth is that nobody would listen.
"Clerk Brandt is suspended pending review," says the chair. "Her pass, please. And the warrant fid."
I unhook the fid from my belt. There is still a twist of string on it where the docket was tied. I lay it on the table next to my pass, and I thank them for hearing me, because you do.
There's a man waiting in the corridor outside. Grey suit, good shoes, a face already smiling at me.

"Ila," he says. "It is Ila? Gervase Vosper. Field Allocation. Senior Knotter, for my sins." He offers his hand. "I countersigned your warrant, so I feel rather responsible for you. Would you do me the kindness of letting me walk you down?"
Nobody senior has ever walked me anywhere. I say yes.
On the stairs he tells me my report was the cleanest he's read this year. "Proper handwriting. You hardly see it now."
"Can I ask you something?" I say. "Why did Allocation countersign it? An anonymous complaint, sent to a clerk. It isn't usual."

"No, it isn't," he agrees, warmly, as if I've said something clever. "Allocation had nobody spare, and Registry had you. Call it a favour to both of us. I'll have a word with Standards about your drawer, if you like. I can't promise anything. But I can ask."
"Would you? Oh, thank you."
"Then tell me something in return. How did your two fall, in the end? I always ask a knotter about their first. It's the one you remember."
So I tell him. The pipe, the foreman, the drawer, the box. He laughs in the right places, kindly.
"And yesterday, on the steps," he says. "Did anyone near you have any unusual luck?"

So I tell him that too. The nurse who stepped out of the tram queue. The defibrillator in the shelter. The ambulance already waiting at the lights. All three, unasked. I tell him about the half-turn, and I tell him my name came over the ambulance radio, because Mr Pargeter said so and it has been going round my head all night. I tell him in full, because he's the first person in the building who has listened.
At the bottom of the stairs he is quiet for a moment. Then he holds the door to Tallow Row open for me.
"Thank you, Ila," he says. "That's very generous of you. Truly."
Outside it is raining the way it rains in Brindlemouth in March. Across the road, in the tram shelter, in his borrowed coat, with his leather case between his feet, is Mr Pargeter.
He said he would wait. I didn't think he meant all day.
He crosses over and looks at my belt, where the fid isn't.
"They've let you go," he says.
"Suspended," I say. "Pending review. Not because of you. Because of a drawer."
"Ah," he says. "In my day they gave you a medal for losing things." He tilts his head. "And has your rope come down yet?"
It takes me a moment. My slack. Nobody has called it the rope since before the manuals I learned from were printed. Another old word, like the spike.
"This morning," I say. "A pipe."
"Good," he says. "Then you're clear of it, and you can go somewhere for me." He takes a scrap of paper from his coat pocket, folded small, and presses it into my hand.
It's the same slanting hand as his complaint. The top terrace, Nettlecombe Allotments. Ask for Orla.
"Who's Orla?" I ask.
"A gardener."
"Is she a knotter?"
"Never heard the word," says Mr Pargeter, and hums.
I am suspended, I am soaked to the skin, and I am holding an address from a man I watched die yesterday.
"Ask for Orla," he says. "Tell her the umbrellas stopped. And Miss Brandt? She won't be pleased."
